claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by its simple single-phase solid-solution state.
The single-phase CoCrFeNiTi state lacks significant lattice distortion.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state contains minimal or no strengthening second-phase precipitates.
Lattice distortion and second-phase precipitates normally impede dislocation motion.
Deformation of the starting alloy is dominated by facile dislocation glide.
Facile dislocation glide produces high plasticity and machinability but low resistance to plastic flow.
The applicable composition is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting alloy likely has coarse grains.
Thermomechanical treatment can refine the grains or form precipitates in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Grain refinement or precipitate formation introduces additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
The comparison is to be conducted under quasi-static room-temperature loading, with elevated-temperature tests optional.
The absence of fine grains or second phases minimizes dislocation pinning and forest hardening.
The absence of lattice-distortion and precipitation strengthening lowers hardness and yield strength.
As-cast single-phase CoCrFeNiTi will have lower Vickers hardness and yield strength than treated material containing refined grains or precipitates.
As-cast single-phase CoCrFeNiTi will maintain high ductility.
Strengthening by grain refinement or precipitate formation should cause a corresponding decrease in ductility.
At room-temperature quasi-static loading, diffusion-mediated processes are not dominant.
Failure of the treated samples to show a significant hardness and yield-strength increase, together with reduced ductility, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
